body.title: Training the Body
body.subtitle: 7 days to make the body the mind’s ally

body.title: The body is a tool too
body.read:
The alarm goes off. The duvet is warm, the room is cold. Five more minutes. Then ten. By the time you get up, the day has already started dragging you along.

Musonius Rufus used to tell his students: a human being is neither soul alone nor body alone; the two work together. That is why the philosopher trains the body too: to get used to cold, heat, hunger, thirst and a hard bed. The aim is not to look strong; it is that when discomfort knocks, it doesn’t get to make the decision.

This isn’t a fitness program. No muscles, no weight, no numbers. What the Stoics called “askēsis” meant, in Greek, the regular practice of a craftsman or an athlete; they carried the word over to character. For Musonius, some exercises belong to the soul alone, and some to soul and body together; this week you’ll work with the second kind.

The archer who strings the bow a little every day doesn’t do it to break the bow. It’s so the hand won’t shake when it matters.

This week you’ll do small things. They’ll work precisely because they are small.

This program is not medical or fitness advice. If you have a health condition, talk to your doctor before trying this week’s practices.
body.body: Today, notice and write down three moments when you ran away from discomfort: cold, hunger, tiredness, boredom. Don’t change any of them; just see them.
body.ask: Which of your decisions did discomfort make for you today?

body.title: Walk and think
body.read:
You’re reading the same sentence at your desk for the third time. Your head is full, but no thought reaches its end. You get up, go to the window, then sit down again.

The Stoics take their name from a building: a colonnade in Athens whose walls were decorated with paintings, the Stoa Poikile. Zeno taught there, pacing up and down between the columns. Seneca writes it too: we should take walks in the open air; the wide sky and deep breathing gather the mind and lift it.

This isn’t walking to empty your head. Whoever tries to empty their head usually fills it with their phone. As you walk, you carry a single question; your steps turn it over for you. Most answers come not while you’re sitting, but on the second half of the way.

Running water gathers no moss.

When you get back, you’ll sit at the same desk. But not the same person will sit there.
body.body: Walk for 15 minutes without your phone or headphones. Carry a single question with you: “What opportunity is hidden in the thing that is challenging me today?” When you get back, write one sentence.
body.ask: Where did the question go while you were walking? Did you reach a place you couldn’t reach sitting down?

body.title: One step into cold water
body.read:
Warm water is running in the shower; outside it’s cold. For a moment you think about turning the tap to cold, then you change your mind. Why bother?

In a letter written in his old age, Seneca laughs at himself: he used to greet the new year by plunging into Rome’s cold aqueduct canal on the first day of January, and called himself a “great cold-water lover”. Over time he moved first to the Tiber, then to his own tub; and now even that tub, he says, is warmed by the sun. Without shame, knowing his measure.

There are two lessons here. First: a small, voluntary cold is a rehearsal for the big colds life will bring without asking. You learn that the place where your body says “I can’t take it” is a little further than you thought. Second: this isn’t a show. Even Seneca listened to his own body.

The smith takes the blade out of the fire and plunges it into water. The water lasts only a moment; that is what hardens the steel.

Thirty seconds. Then warm again. But for one short moment in those thirty seconds, the decision is yours.

If you have heart or blood pressure problems, if you are pregnant, or if being cold doesn’t agree with you, just wash your face and wrists instead of taking a cold shower.
body.body: Finish your shower with 30 seconds of cold water. If you don’t want to, wash your face and wrists with cold water; that counts too.
body.ask: When the cold came, what was the first thing that spoke up inside you? What happened next?

body.title: A simple table
body.read:
Lunch. Fork in one hand, phone in the other. The plate is empty; you don’t remember what you ate, and you didn’t quite feel full either.

When Musonius talks about food, he recalls Socrates: most people live to eat; I eat to live. For him, simple food that is easy to find keeps both body and mind light; whoever learns measure at the table learns it elsewhere too.

This isn’t a diet. No one is telling you what to eat; there are no numbers, no bans, no lists. Only this: be present with what you eat. Speed and screens steal both the taste and the feeling of being full.

To a hungry person, dry bread tastes sweeter than a feast. Taste isn’t only on the plate; it’s also in what you bring to the table.

One meal. One plate. Slowly. Maybe you’ll taste it for the first time in years.
body.body: Today, eat one meal without a screen, from a single plate, and slowly. For the first three bites, pay attention only to the taste.
body.ask: In the meal you ate slowly and without a screen, what did you notice: the taste, feeling full, or boredom?

body.title: Let no one see
body.read:
You’re waiting in front of the lift. The stairs are right next to it. For a moment you think “I’ll take the stairs”, then you give up because no one will see. Or the opposite: you take them and want someone to notice.

When Epictetus talks about training, he points to this second trap: don’t do your exercise so others will see it. When you’re thirsty, take a mouthful of cold water, spit it out, and tell no one. Effort that is put on display stops being effort; hardship endured for applause trains the show, not the character.

That’s why today’s practice is silent. No sharing, no telling, no “here’s what I did today”. Only you will know.

The tree whose roots grow under the soil is the one that stands firmest in the wind.

A small effort no one knows about leaves you a strength no one can take away.
body.body: Choose a small effort that no one will see: the stairs instead of the lift, standing instead of sitting while you wait, waiting patiently in a queue. Don’t tell anyone.
body.ask: With no one watching, did this effort feel harder or easier?

body.title: Short and simple
body.read:
You’re hunched over the screen. Your neck has slid forward, your shoulders have crept up toward your ears. You don’t know how long you’ve been sitting like this.

Seneca advises his friend not to neglect the body, but not to give it too much time either: let the body’s exercise be short and easy; running, a light weight in the hands, a jump. Things that tire the body quickly and don’t steal your time. Then return to the mind at once.

This isn’t blaming people who don’t go to the gym. Quite the opposite: because it’s neither long nor hard, there’s nothing to put off. Five minutes is enough. What matters is remembering that your body is there, and not letting tension pile up.

A hand kept clenched all day forgets how to open in the evening.

In five minutes you’ll go back to the screen. But your shoulders won’t be up by your ears; they’ll be where they belong.

If you feel pain or dizziness, or have an injury, stop the movement; forcing it is no part of this program.
body.body:
Five minutes, four movements. Slowly, without rushing:
1. Tilt your head slowly to the right, then to the left; stay for three breaths on each side.
2. Roll your shoulders backward five times.
3. Stretch your arms overhead, interlace your fingers, and reach up for three breaths.
4. Stand up, place your hands behind your lower back, and gently open your chest.
When you finish: unclench your jaw, let your shoulders drop, open your hands.
body.ask: Where did your body tense up most during the day? When did you notice it?

body.title: Measure
body.read:
It’s been a week. Maybe you came to like the cold water, maybe the walk. Maybe now you want to do everything at once, build a program, keep track of numbers.

Here Epictetus puts on the brakes: spending a lot of time on the body, on exercise, on eating and drinking, is the sign of a dull mind. These things should be done along the way; the real place for your attention is the mind. The body is a tool, not the goal.

This doesn’t undo the week. A tool should be kept in good shape; but whoever worships the tool forgets the work. The Stoics didn’t train the body for show, but so it would be a tool for living well: to be resilient, to be ready when needed, and not to stand in the mind’s way.

A scribe sharpens the pen every day, but doesn’t spend the whole day sharpening it. The real work is writing.

Let one thing remain from this week: small, chosen by you, coming back once a week. Leave the rest to the mind.
body.body: Choose the one practice from this week that felt best. Let it be “your own askēsis”, done once a week; write down its name and its day.
body.ask: What did your body teach you about your mind this week?
